library(DrugScreenExplorer)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(gridExtra)
library(ggplot2)
library(tools)

1 Installation

The DrugScreenExplorer package can be installed from Bioconductor using the following commands:


if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("DrugScreenExplorer")

2 Introduction

DrugScreenExplorer offers an intuitive R Shiny application, empowering users of all technical backgrounds to conduct comprehensive drug screen analyses through an interactive web interface. The application seamlessly integrates all functionalities of the underlying R package within its user-friendly graphical interface.

With just a few clicks, this R Shiny app allows users to effortlessly:

  • Import and merge raw drug screening datasets
  • Process and normalize the resulting data
  • Adjust the potential bias due to edge effects
  • Summarize dose-response effects
  • Analyze the synergy or antagonism effects of two-drug combination
  • Explore the relationship between drug response and features

3 Initiate the Shiny Application

There are two ways to start the Shiny Application:

1 Execute *runShiny()* function directly

This approach requires organizing all input files - including well annotations, plate annotations, and raw screening data - into structured folders with specific naming conventions. The entire directory structure should then be compressed into a single ZIP archive for import into the Shiny application.

Shiny Data/
├── plateAnno
├── rawData
└── wellAnno

The files within these three folders must adhere to the format specifications required by the readScreen() function. For guidance on preparing these files, please consult the following functions in our documentation:The files within these three folders must adhere to the format specifications required by the readScreen() function. For guidance on preparing these files, please consult the following functions in our documentation:

  • readScreen() - Read and assemble a drug screen dataset
  • createWellInput() - Create a template for well annotation file
  • createPlateInput() - Create a template for plate annotation file

Fortunately, the DrugScreenExplorer package incorporated a function (createShinyData) to generate the required data within one-step.

createShinyData(rawDir, plateAnnotationFile, wellAnnotationFile, dir = ".")

2 Run *makeShiny()* function

The second strategy to start the Shiny application is to run makeShiny() function. The function create a directory comprising R shiny script and required data. We can directly start the Shiny application by running the generated script using R.

4 First-look of the Shiny Application

The Shiny application contains the following tabs:

  • Data preprocessing - Includes data import, normalization, and correction for edge effects.
  • Plate Plot - Provides an overview of each plate.
  • Dose-response curves - Visualizes dose-response curves for selected drugs and samples.
  • Clustering - Shows similarities between drugs or samples.
  • Association test- Examines relationships with sample information.
  • Overview Two-Drug Combination - Summarizes of two-drug combinations.
  • Durg Combination Effects - Illustrates the effects resulting from two-drug combinations.

5 Data preprocessing

5.1 Data import

As mentioned earlier, the Shiny application imports a ZIP file generated by compressing a structured folder containing well annotations, plate annotations, and raw screening data. This compressed file can be directly created using the createShinyData() function.

Once the path to the compressed data is specified, several additional parameters must be configured before importing:

  • The row and column ranges containing the actual values;
  • The separator between these values;
  • Whether commas is used as the decimal.

These are indeed required arguments in readScreen() function. Please refer to the help document of readScreen() for information.

After setting these options, clicking the “Import” button will load and combine all data into a single table. Upon successful import, the right panel will display an overview of all samples. Additional details can be viewed by selecting specific sample information.

5.2 Normalization

Adapted from normalizePlate() function, this R Shiny application offers two normalization methods: ‘negatives’ or ‘NPI’. The ‘negatives’ method requires specifying negative controls, while ‘NPI’ needs both negative and positive drug information For details, please refer to the normalizePlate() function documentation. Note that normalization can be a time-consuming process; please be patient.

This procedure will return and display a table containing the following default columns:

  • SampleID
  • fileName
  • wellID
  • rowID
  • colID
  • drug name
  • original values
  • normalized values

Additional columns can be included by selecting the desired options under “Select sample information to display”. These columns might be indispensable when exploring the relationship between drug effects and sample annotations in the Association test panel.

5.3 Edge effects Adjustment

The final step in data processing is edge effect adjustment, performed by the correctEdgeEffect() function. Currently, two methods are supported for estimating edge effects:

  • ‘loess’: Uses a local regression model to estimate edge effects.
  • ‘sigmoid’: An experimental feature that applies a 2D-sigmoid model for estimation.

This adjustment process is also computationally intensive. Upon completion, a new column named normVal.cor will be added to the normalized data table.

6 Visualize the drug screen plate

The Plate plot panel displays a heatmap of a selected plate, showing values such as viability, adjusted viability, z-score, or raw count. Detailed information for each well can be accessed by clicking on it in the heatmap. This action generates a table containing comprehensive drug information and a line plot illustrating how the selected value changes across different concentrations of the corresponding drug.

7 Explore the dose-response effects of drugs

With the panel Clustering samples or drugs based on drug response, users can easily explore the similarity between samples or drugs. The similarity can be calculated based on three drug effect summarization measures: average viability, AUC, and IC50.

The Shiny application provides several methods to assess and visualize these similarities. Among them, hierarchical clustering and correlation analysis are intuitive approaches for measuring similarity, and the results are visualized using heatmaps.

PCA was applied to the drug effect summarization values to extract principal components. The first two components, which capture the largest variance, were visualized using scatter plots to illustrate the distances between samples or drugs. Similarly, t-SNE was used to project the high-dimensional data into a two-dimensional space. The resulting embeddings were displayed in scatter plots, highlighting relative distances and clustering patterns.

8 Test associations between drug responses and sample annotations

The R shiny application enables a simple exploration on the association between the obtained drug responses (i.e., average viability, AUC, and IC50) to a specific sample annotations.

The sample annotation can be binary, categorical, or continuous. For binary annotations, a Student’s t-test will be performed, supporting both equal and unequal variance assumptions. The results, including mean differences, p-values, and adjusted p-values are summarized in a table. By clicking on a row, a box plot will be generated to visualize the distribution between the two groups.

Anova test will be performed for a categorical annotation variable, and a similar boxplot will be drawn for each drug.

For continuous sample annotation variables, correlation with drug responses will be calculated. Spearman correlation will be used as a non-parametric alternative to Pearson correlation. The relationship can be visualized using scatter plots with fitted trend lines to illustrate the association between variables and drug response.

If Edge Effects Adjustment is performed in the Data Preprocessing panel, an option for Incubation Effect Correction will become available. When selected, it enables the use of edge-effect corrected drug responses in the association test.

9 Using Shiny Application to explore the two-drug combination effects

Once a drug2 column was detected in the well annotation profile, the R Shiny application automatically switches to the mode designed for exploring two-drug combination effects.

In the current version, there are four panels available: Data Preprocessing, Plate Plot, Overview of Two-drug Combination, and Drug combination effects.

The Data preprocessing procedure is the same as when handling a single drug, except for specifying the negative control wells and positive wells. In two-drug combinations, the drug names are linked by an underscore.

Plate plot panel is also similar to that in the single-drug scenario. By clicking a well in the heatmap, the trend of drug effects across concentrations will be displayed in a two-dimensional plot

The Overview of Two-Drug Combination panel summarizes and visualizes the effects of two-drug combinations estimated using either the bliss or bayesynergy methods.

When the bliss method is applied, two types of combination indices are available:

  • CI: Combination Index
  • logCI: Log-transformed Combination Index

The CI is defined as: \(CI = viabObs - viabExp\), where viabObs and viabExp are Observed viability and Expected viability.

  • If \(CI > 0\): Antagonism
  • If \(CI = 0\): Additive / Independent
  • If \(CI < 0\): Synergy

Likelywise, logCI is defined as \(logCI = log10(viabObs / viabExp)\).

  • If \(logCI > 0\): Antagonism (Observed viability > Expected)
  • If \(logCI = 0\): Additive / Independent
  • If \(logCI < 0\): Synergy (Observed viability < Expected)

Of note, the bayesynergy package need to be installed manually from https://github.com/ocbe-uio/bayesynergy if bayesynergy methods is selected to assess the drug combination effects.

The Drug Combination Effects panel enables the visualization of combination effects. For the Bliss method, three types of plots are available: the Dose–Response Curve, which compares observed versus expected viability across concentrations; the Scatter Plot, which displays the relationship between observed and expected viability at different concentrations; and the Box Plot, which illustrates the distribution of the combination index across different samples.

For the bayesynergy method, the R Shiny application provides two main visualization plots: “Synergy Against Antagonism” and “Pairwise Drug Interaction”, which can display results averaged across all samples or for individual samples. Additionally, the “Synergy Per Experiment ID” plot summarizes synergy effects by sample.

The “Synergy Against Antagonism” plot displays synergy and antagonism effects of different drug combinations in a scatter plot. Meanwhile, the “Pairwise Drug Interaction” plot provides an overview of synergy effects for all drug pairs.

All generated plots can be downloaded in PDF format to a local repository.
